attribution_limitations: The reported timeline of discharge and the fracture is not self-consistent: the infant was 9 days old at NICU transfer and hospitalized for 9 days (respiratory support stopped on day 18 of life), yet the fracture is dated both to the 16th day after discharge and to the 25th day of life.
The article states that follow-up findings met the criteria for harness removal but does not state that the Pavlik harness was removed or when.

The settings and details of nCPAP are stated in the discussion and a figure caption without a stated start time; the discussion says nCPAP followed deterioration and CT evidence of worsening pneumonia.

evidence.quote: (A) Whole-exome sequencing (WES) of amniotic fluid cells from the proband, revealing a heterozygous c.1459G > A mutation in the COL1A2 gene (red arrow).
(B,C) Sanger sequencing validation within the family, confirming the mutation was inherited from the affected father (B)
while the mother was wild-type (C)

Figure 2
Sanger sequencing confirmation of the COL1A2 mutation in the proband. Postnatal Sanger sequencing validation confirmed the presence of the heterozygous c.1459G > A mutation (red arrow) in the proband's peripheral blood DNA. This missense mutation leads to the substitution of glycine by arginine at position 487 (p.Gly487Arg) within the highly conserved triple-helical domain of the collagen α2(I) chain. Such structural mutations are typically associated with a severe type III OI phenotype.
(A) diffuse osteopenia and thinning of the cranial vault.
(B) Generalized osteopenia of the long bones, thin cortices, relatively widened medullary cavities, and flared metaphyses; slender and curved bilateral clavicles are also evident.
(C) Loss of normal spinal curvatures.

Figure 4
The infant received nasal Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (nCPAP) with the following parameters: positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) 5 cmH_(2)O, fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO_(2)) 30%.
(A) (AP view): a fracture line with slight angulation is visible in the proximal right femur (red arrow).
(B) (FroG–Leg lateral view): the inherent bony abnormalities of OI, including bowing and thin cortices, are also seen.
(A) Clinical photograph showing the infant with both lower limbs immobilized in a Pavlik harness.
(B) Corresponding right femur radiograph taken with the harness in place, confirming maintained fracture alignment under fixation.

Figure 7
Radiographic evidence of rapid fracture healing (day 52 of life). Follow-up radiograph of the right femur reveals: satisfactory fracture alignment with a blurred fracture line and abundant cloud-like callus formation surrounding the site (red arrow). This image exemplifies the characteristic “rapid and hyperplastic” callus formation ability in OI, indicating successful initial healing and meeting the criteria for harness removal.

Figure 8
Radiographic outcome at the final follow-up (day 136 of life). Final follow-up radiograph of the right femur demonstrates complete bony union with remodeling and consolidation of the previously formed callus (red arrow). Despite fracture healing, the underlying bony deformity and bowing of the femur persist. This image shows the final outcome of the fracture and underscores the persistent nature of the skeletal abnormalities in OI, which coexist with the fracture healing process.

limitations: Caption-layer visual status not_inspected; the eight images are described in the separate visual submission.

claims.text: A 9-day-old male neonate with a prenatally identified paternally inherited heterozygous COL1A2 c.1459G > A (p.Gly487Arg) mutation, born by cesarean section at 34 weeks after prenatal ultrasound findings suggestive of OI, was transferred to the NICU in January 2025 for persistent respiratory distress. He had tachypnea of 56 breaths per minute, retractions, thoracoabdominal asynchrony, bilateral rales, oxygen saturation declining to 85%, bilateral knee valgus deformities and lower limb bowing, with non-blue sclerae, elevated interleukin-6 and normal calcium, phosphate and ALP. Sanger sequencing confirmed the mutation and skeletal survey radiographs showed generalized osteopenia, thin cortices and bowing. Normal calcium, phosphate and ALP helped rule out metabolic bone disease.

Figure 1
Prenatal genetic diagnosis and familial segregation. (A) Whole-exome sequencing (WES) of amniotic fluid cells from the proband, revealing a heterozygous c.1459G > A mutation in the COL1A2 gene (red arrow). (B,C) Sanger sequencing validation within the family, confirming the mutation was inherited from the affected father (B), while the mother was wild-type (C) This figure establishes the genetic etiology of the disease, providing the definitive basis for prenatal diagnosis and postnatal precision management.

evidence.quote:
Figure 1
Prenatal genetic diagnosis and familial segregation. (A) Whole-exome sequencing (WES) of amniotic fluid cells from the proband, revealing a heterozygous c.1459G > A mutation in the COL1A2 gene (red arrow). (B,C) Sanger sequencing validation within the family, confirming the mutation was inherited from the affected father (B), while the mother was wild-type (C) This figure establishes the genetic etiology of the disease, providing the definitive basis for prenatal diagnosis and postnatal precision management.

caption_claims.text:
Figure 2
Sanger sequencing confirmation of the COL1A2 mutation in the proband. Postnatal Sanger sequencing validation confirmed the presence of the heterozygous c.1459G > A mutation (red arrow) in the proband's peripheral blood DNA. This missense mutation leads to the substitution of glycine by arginine at position 487 (p.Gly487Arg) within the highly conserved triple-helical domain of the collagen α2(I) chain. Such structural mutations are typically associated with a severe type III OI phenotype.

caption_claims.text:
Figure 3
Initial radiographic skeletal survey at admission (Day 9 of life). Full-body radiographs demonstrate the classic imaging features of severe, type III OI: (A) diffuse osteopenia and thinning of the cranial vault. (B) Generalized osteopenia of the long bones, thin cortices, relatively widened medullary cavities, and flared metaphyses; slender and curved bilateral clavicles are also evident. (C) Loss of normal spinal curvatures. These findings form the radiographic basis for the diagnosis of OI in the neonatal period and explain the inherent high fracture risk.
